title: Other power
hook: Shinran: awakening comes through Amida's power, not our own effort

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tanluan and Shandao: the books on long life burned, the white path between fire and water. Your line was the Chinese masters. Did you name who taught you something? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

A monk comes down a mountain. Tradition says Shinran spent long years training on Mount Hiei, the monastery mountain above Kyoto: study, chanting, long nights of practice. And he came down convinced that none of it had changed what was wrong inside him. In the city he found Honen, the teacher of the nembutsu, and stayed. Later, a disciple wrote down what Shinran said about that choice: even if Honen had misled him, and saying the name led him to hell, he would have no regret, because no other practice had ever been within his reach. Today's word is what he was leaning on: tariki.
screen: `A MONK COMES DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.` → `HE FINDS HONEN.` → `NO OTHER PRACTICE WAS WITHIN REACH.`

segments.voice: First, two words. Jiriki means self power: awakening built by your own effort, your discipline, your merit. Tariki means other power: the power of Amida's vow, working on you from outside your own effort. Yesterday the easy path was a boat, the image Tanluan took from Nagarjuna. Tariki is the boat. Second, what Shinran did with it. For Shinran, other power reaches all the way down. Not only is the Pure Land Amida's gift; even the trust that receives it, even the nembutsu on your lips, is Amida at work, not a technique you perform well. Third, the line people stop at. The same record of his words, the Tannisho, has him say: even a good person is born in the Pure Land, so how much more an evil person. It sounds backward. The record's explanation: the person who trusts their own goodness is still leaning, a little, on self power. The one who knows they have nothing to offer leans entirely on the vow. Fourth, what it is not. Other power is not an excuse to stop caring how you live; the record has Shinran warning against people who did wrong on purpose because they thought the vow would cover it. And Pure Land teachers differ here. In Honen's Jodo school, the nembutsu is practiced often and earnestly as the practice the vow chose. In Shinran's Jodo Shinshu, the emphasis falls on receiving, not achieving. Both say the name. They place the effort differently. What Shinran found coming down the mountain was not a better method. It was the end of needing one.
screen: `JIRIKI, SELF POWER. TARIKI, OTHER POWER.` · `EVEN THE TRUST IS GIVEN.` · `HOW MUCH MORE AN EVIL PERSON.` · `NOT AN EXCUSE; NOT A METHOD.` · then, large: `OTHER POWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing be done for you. Start right now. Settle into the chair, and notice what is already holding you up: the seat, the floor, the ground under the building. You didn't build any of it. Let the weight go into it. Notice the breath, which keeps going whether you manage it or not. For the rest of the sit, stop helping. Let the chair hold you, and let the breath breathe. The bell holds the time.
Tariki. Other power: in Shin Buddhism, the power of Amida's vow, which does what self power cannot. Today's word.

Your line: other power. Today, let one thing be done for you without fixing it or paying it back right away: a ride, a meal, a door held open. Just receive it. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: In Jodo Shinshu, Shin Buddhists understand birth in the Pure Land as the work of Amida's vow, other power, rather than their own effort; they say the nembutsu, and hear Shinran's teaching in temple talks and in readings from the Tannisho.

original.note: Japanese: tariki, other power, set against jiriki (自力), self power.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone else does the work, so you don't have to.
what it means: in Shinran's teaching, awakening comes through the power of Amida's vow, not through your own effort or merit.
what a scholar hears: Shinran's turn: even the trust and the nembutsu are given, which is why the Tannisho can say 'how much more an evil person.'
